summary:
Systematic Investor 368 (Oct 2025): guest argues markets are driven by supply, demand and liquidity rather than fundamentals; 2025 is like 1998-99, a liquidity-driven bubble with structured product, dealer and positioning flows.
Approach: positioning/dealer-flow reflexivity, long-dated call stock replacement, debasement hedges (gold, crypto), seasonal flow calendar.
Main view: bullish into year-end/mid-January with higher volatility on the upside; inflation is the eventual check.

claims.speaker: Alan
claims.quote: Sockchen CTA was up 3.82% uh leaving it down 2.66 on the year
claims.claim: September 2025: SG CTA +3.82% (YTD -2.66%), SG Trend +5.66% (YTD -2.32%), BTOP50 +3.5% (YTD +0.66%), short-term traders +1.4% (YTD -5%) in an everything rally; gold up close to 12%, S&P +3.6%.
claims.indicator: SG CTA, SG Trend, BTOP50, gold
claims.direction: trends in equities and gold paid

claims.speaker: Jem
claims.quote: valuations are not a a good timing mechanism
claims.claim: Valuations are not a timing tool: fundamentals have little predictive value over horizons under 10 years but become predictive over 10 years; valuation is a risk-management tool, like altitude on an airplane.

claims.speaker: Jem
claims.quote: markets are a function of liquidity
claims.claim: Markets are driven by supply and demand and liquidity, often unrelated to fundamentals, so bubbles reach extreme heights and end only when the 'gas' runs out.

claims.speaker: Jem
claims.quote: structured product issuance uh short interest
claims.claim: Current supply and demand drivers: record structured product issuance (compresses volatility), short interest and relative-value hedge fund growth, momentum releveraging from passive and levered investors, and an administration not incentivized to stop pushing.
claims.indicator: structured product issuance; short interest; hedge fund size

claims.speaker: Jem
claims.quote: there is a ton of real edge by playing the distribution which is really mispriced
claims.claim: The 1998-99 analogue means playing the distribution (options) is mispriced by supply and demand imbalance at the end of a bubble.

claims.speaker: Jem
claims.quote: the inputs for um for a bubble to really get to these heights right is a liquidity push
claims.claim: Bubble inputs: a liquidity push (1996 Greenspan; now loss of Fed independence) and a narrative that 'this time is different' (internet then, AI now).

claims.speaker: Alan
claims.quote: the deficit is one big difference
claims.claim: Differences vs 1999: US deficit not surplus, tariffs, weaker productivity, loss of US hegemony; yet government has bigger toolset and market structure supports.

claims.speaker: Jem
claims.quote: the potential energy for when something does shift is dramatically bigger
claims.claim: Sumo market: two opposing forces make the potential energy of an eventual shift much bigger without saying when.

claims.speaker: Jem
claims.quote: the biggest and most predictable thing in supply and demand the market is the potential buyers and the
claims.claim: Reflexivity in measurable form is positioning: a long world has many sellers and few buyers left; if everyone hedges a 3% decline it probably will not come, and if it does it can reach 12%.

claims.speaker: Jem
claims.quote: that's what a wall of worry is right again if people are worried that means they're underweight the market
claims.claim: A wall of worry means underweight positioning; investors get forced back in, as in summer 2025 and likely into year-end.

claims.speaker: Jem
claims.quote: you have potential energy
claims.claim: A swing one way raises odds of swinging back, not only from the swing but from the stored positioning.

claims.speaker: Jem
claims.quote: hedge fund assets have gone from two and a half to four and a half trillion dollars in just three years
claims.claim: Since stock-bond correlation breakdown in 2022, diversification demand pushed hedge fund assets from 2.5 to 4.5 trillion and structured products from 500 billion to 2 trillion in three years, mostly retail via RIAs and Asia.
claims.indicator: hedge fund AUM; structured product issuance

claims.speaker: Jem
claims.quote: people saw that correlation breakdown stocks and bonds are like well we don't have any diversification
claims.claim: Stock-bond correlation breakdown since 2022 removed bond diversification, driving flows into non-correlated strategies.

claims.speaker: Jem
claims.quote: autocolable type
claims.claim: Autocallable-type structured products make investors short volatility (sellers of vol).

claims.speaker: Jem
claims.quote: How much have we seen in the increase in the valuations of precious metals? A three-fold increase
claims.claim: Hedge funds ~2x, structured products ~4x, precious metals and crypto ~3x over three years: about 15 trillion of non-correlated assets vs 500 trillion of long assets; the shift is in second or third inning.
claims.indicator: non-correlated assets vs long market size
claims.direction: long gold, crypto, hedge fund strategies

claims.speaker: Jem
claims.quote: AI is going to unlock and make a lot of options access uh much easier
claims.claim: AI will make options and structured products accessible, boosting exponential growth and reflexive effects on markets.

claims.speaker: Jem
claims.quote: the biggest provider of liquidity we've talked about the gas and the airplane right is actually markets themselves
claims.claim: Rising markets create collateral and leverage (mortgage example); the system is leverage all the way down; a 20% rise adds ~100 trillion in assets, bigger liquidity than QE.

claims.speaker: Jem
claims.quote: it is more the dog than the tail
claims.claim: The market is the dog, not the tail: in 2000 the market fall caused 95% of tech to fail and a recession; markets drive the economy through liquidity.

claims.speaker: Jem
claims.quote: you start to see volatility increase into a rally
claims.claim: At the end of a bubble volatility rises with the rally because upside moves get huge; demand for upside protection rises, creating a self-reinforcing loop (Burns/Nixon 1970s).

claims.speaker: Jem
claims.quote: the ultimate check on that environment is inflation
claims.claim: Inflation is the ultimate check on liquidity-driven markets because government cannot control it, especially when the Fed abandons rules-based smoothing.

claims.speaker: Jem
claims.quote: one of the best times in history to be long longdated calls
claims.claim: In 1998-99 long-dated calls made money on the way up and the way down; they unpin markets and eventually raise inflation.

claims.speaker: Jem
claims.quote: you can't keep real interest rates that negative or negative really at all for quite a time
claims.claim: Persistent negative real rates drive leveraged borrowing into appreciating assets and feed inflation (1970s); best hedges are non-inflation-controlled assets: precious metals, crypto, debasement trades, not breakevens.

claims.speaker: Jem
claims.quote: in the short term um control full control right of the administration who is incentivized
claims.claim: Short term, an incentivized administration controls asset reflation into midterms; this lasts until inflation breaks it.

claims.speaker: Jem
claims.quote: if you're predicting markets, as we said, it's not about fundamentals. It's about supply and
claims.claim: Predict markets via supply and demand and who controls demand, not long-term realities.

claims.speaker: Jem
claims.quote: longdated calls are dramatically underpriced relative to the risks on the right tail
claims.claim: Right-tail (long-dated calls) skew is underpriced given debasement, institutional net-short and structured product flows; bubbles are leptokurtic with a later left tail.

claims.speaker: Jem
claims.quote: Why would you own the whole distribution right?
claims.claim: Replace stock with out-of-the-money calls (stock replacement): short the left tail and underweight the right? Buy the cheapest part of the distribution (112% strike calls, vol ~ avg 17).

claims.speaker: Jem
claims.quote: We are seeing market up, volume up, market up, volume up
claims.claim: Market-up/vol-up for a year is unprecedented since 2001; it is an easy way to make money in the vol space.

claims.speaker: Jem
claims.quote: the best performing asset by far it's not even close was was
claims.claim: During 1968-1982 inflation era the best asset was gold (also most volatile, two-way); equities went nowhere because inflation hits valuation multiples; FX and precious metals are related.

claims.speaker: Jem
claims.quote: crypto is going to continue to perform well but it is not going to be a straight line
claims.claim: Crypto will keep performing but with high volatility and could go vertical; gold calls expensive but volatility broadly still cheap.

claims.speaker: Jem
claims.quote: the way people are betting on AI is very one-dimensional
claims.claim: AI betting is first-order thinking, like 1999 socks.com; winners are unknown, profits probably will not accrue to AI itself (commoditized) but to unique data sets and inputs (energy, power, data).
claims.direction: favour data and energy over AI labs

claims.speaker: Jem
claims.quote: the one who controls data again for individuals and for companies
claims.claim: The AI platform winner likely controls data; cheap sectors with unique data sets, e.g. UnitedHealth/healthcare, offer asymmetric payoff.

claims.speaker: Jem
claims.quote: options are the true underlying
claims.claim: Options give a full distribution (3D trading) and will become accessible through AI; beneficiaries are brokers, exchanges (margin up with inflation), market makers and platforms.

claims.speaker: Jem
claims.quote: the edges are decaying because AI takes away some of the um you know the value of of that knowledge
claims.claim: AI commoditizes data edges for pod shops but a tide of new AI entrants may widen spreads, so winners and losers change.

claims.speaker: Jem
claims.quote: We've gone from $20 billion of those just three years ago
claims.claim: Options-based ETF assets grew from 20bn to 300bn in three years, 15x, driven by RIAs (the biggest pool of assets).

claims.speaker: Jem
claims.quote: the structured product issuance is dramatically bigger than it was last year
claims.claim: Seasonal patterns are driven by structural flows that are growing; headlines matter only for massive left-tail events (COVID declines only began in February after opex).
claims.indicator: structured products, hedge fund long/short size

claims.speaker: Jem
claims.quote: Markets are up 15% for the year. you have five, you know, 200 trillion of equities
claims.claim: Year-end flows: a $30 trillion new-year input with ~10% (~$3 trillion) put to work versus ~$100bn daily turnover explains Santa Claus and January effects, the most positive four weeks.

claims.speaker: Jem
claims.quote: institutional position was at the zero percentile in July in June, sorry. Now it's at the 25th
claims.claim: Institutional equity positioning was at the 0th percentile in June and 25th now, so underweight institutions need to chase to keep up (not just equal weight) through year end.

claims.speaker: Jem
claims.quote: structured product is twice as much effect
claims.claim: Summer volume drop doubles the effect of structured product volatility compression (summer of George), charm flows from rehedging are larger than ever.

claims.speaker: Jem
claims.quote: that goes till about the middle of January
claims.claim: Roadmap: bullish into mid-January (January effect, Jan OPEX), front-run seasonal, sideways period, pullback January-February, support into midterm year; the season is on steroids.
